config.title: Build typed shared UI package API

intro.title: Build typed shared UI package API
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a typed API for a shared UI package, which is a collection of reusable components like buttons and inputs. You'll learn how to use TypeScript interfaces to define strict contracts for the props each component accepts, ensuring type safety. The main technologies involved are TypeScript interfaces and generic types to create flexible, reusable component definitions. By the end, you'll have a foundational package structure that can be shared across projects with full type checking and autocompletion.
intro.usecase: This pattern is essential when building component libraries like Material-UI, Ant Design, or internal design systems at companies like Airbnb or Shopify. Developers use typed shared UI packages to create consistent, reusable components such as buttons, modals, and data tables across multiple applications. For example, a dashboard application might import a typed Chart component that enforces proper data structure validation, while an e-commerce platform ensures all product cards have consistent props. This approach prevents bugs during integration and provides excellent developer experience through autocomplete and type checking in IDEs.

objectives: Construct a TypeScript package configuration for shared UI components
Implement typed component interfaces with explicit prop definitions
Configure module exports for type-safe component consumption
Apply generic types to create reusable UI component utilities
Initialize a type declaration file for package-wide type exports
Integrate strict TypeScript compiler options for UI package development
Render type-safe component examples with proper prop validation

steps.title: Import TypeScript types and utilities
steps.instruction: Import React and the necessary TypeScript types that will be used throughout this lesson on building typed UI components.
steps.hint: Start by importing React from 'react'. This is the foundation for creating React components with TypeScript.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: importing React for a TypeScript component
import React from 'react';
steps.seedCode: // Import React and TypeScript types here
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have the basic imports needed to start building typed UI components with React and TypeScript.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've imported React from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's start with the basics. Import React from 'react' to begin building typed UI components.

steps.title: Create a base ButtonProps interface
steps.instruction: Create an interface named ButtonProps with two properties: label of type string and disabled of type boolean.
steps.hint: Use the interface keyword followed by the interface name and define the properties with their types.
steps.seedCode:
// Import React and TypeScript types here

// Create the ButtonProps interface here
steps.expectedOutcome: An interface named ButtonProps with label and disabled properties will be created.
successCriteria: The ButtonProps interface is defined with label: string and disabled: boolean.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure both label and disabled properties are included with the correct types.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface is missing or incorrect. Check that you've defined ButtonProps with both required properties.

steps.title: Extend ButtonProps with variant types
steps.instruction: Add a 'variant' property to the ButtonProps interface using a union type of 'primary' | 'secondary'.
steps.hint: Use the union type syntax with the pipe character (|) to define possible string literal values for the variant property.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ButtonProps interface now includes a variant property that accepts only 'primary' or 'secondary' string values.
successCriteria: ButtonProps interface has a variant property defined with union type 'primary' | 'secondary'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a variant property, but check the union type syntax - it should be 'primary' | 'secondary'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The ButtonProps interface doesn't have a properly typed variant property. Try adding 'variant: "primary" | "secondary";' to the interface.

steps.title: Create a typed Button component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named Button that accepts ButtonProps as its props and returns a button element.
steps.hint: Define a React component using either a function declaration or arrow function that takes ButtonProps as its parameter and returns JSX for a button.
steps.expectedOutcome: A Button component is defined with typed props and returns a button element.
successCriteria: Button component is created, accepts ButtonProps, and returns a button element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a typed Button component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the Button component, but make sure it accepts ButtonProps and returns a button element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Button component is missing or doesn't match the required structure.

steps.title: Add onClick handler type to ButtonProps
steps.instruction: Add an optional onClick property to the ButtonProps interface with the correct React event type for button clicks.
steps.hint: Use React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement> as the event type and make the property optional with ?.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ButtonProps interface will include an optional onClick property typed for button click events.
successCriteria: ButtonProps has an optional onClick property with type (event: React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>) => void.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure onClick is optional (using ?) and has the correct event type: React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>.
steps.feedbackWrong: The onClick property is missing or has incorrect typing. It should be optional and accept a React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement> event.

steps.title: Implement the Button component markup
steps.instruction: Inside the Button component, return a JSX button element that uses the variant prop to set its className and the children prop for its content.
steps.hint: Use the variant prop to conditionally apply CSS classes (like 'primary' or 'secondary') and render children inside the button.
steps.expectedOutcome: The Button component returns a button element with dynamic className based on variant and renders children.
successCriteria: The button JSX element uses the variant prop for className and children prop for content.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the button element uses both variant and children props correctly in JSX.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Button component markup is not implemented correctly. Ensure you return a button element with className={variant} and children inside.

steps.title: Create a CardProps interface with children
steps.instruction: Create a new interface named CardProps with a required title property of type string and a required children property of type React.ReactNode.
steps.hint: Define an interface with two properties: title (string) and children (React.ReactNode).
steps.expectedOutcome: A new CardProps interface is added to the file with the correct property types.
successCriteria: The CardProps interface exists with title: string and children: React.ReactNode properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created an interface, but check that both properties (title and children) have the correct types.
steps.feedbackWrong: The CardProps interface is missing or has incorrect property types. Ensure it has title: string and children: React.ReactNode.

steps.title: Implement the Card component
steps.instruction: Create a Card functional component that accepts CardProps and returns a div element containing a title and children.
steps.hint: Define a Card component using const Card = (props: CardProps) => { ... } that returns JSX with the title and children.
steps.expectedOutcome: A Card component is defined with proper TypeScript typing that renders a title and children.
successCriteria: The Card component is created with CardProps as its parameter type and returns JSX containing the title and children.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the Card component, but make sure it accepts CardProps and returns JSX with both title and children.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Card component is missing or doesn't match the required structure. Check that it accepts CardProps and renders title and children.

steps.title: Create an index.ts export file
steps.instruction: Create an index.ts file that exports the Button and Card components along with their prop types.
steps.hint: Use named exports to export both components and their interfaces from your index.ts file.
steps.expectedOutcome: An index.ts file is created with exports for Button, ButtonProps, Card, and CardProps.
successCriteria: The index.ts file exports Button, ButtonProps, Card, and CardProps using named exports.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're exporting all four items: Button, ButtonProps, Card, and CardProps.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you're creating an index.ts file with proper named exports for both components and their prop types.

steps.title: Test the typed components in a sample usage
steps.instruction: Create a new file named 'sample-usage.tsx' that imports and uses the Button and Card components with proper typing.
steps.hint: Create a new file, import the components from './index', and render them with different props to verify type safety.
steps.expectedOutcome: A new file 'sample-usage.tsx' is created that demonstrates proper usage of the typed Button and Card components.
successCriteria: The file imports Button and Card from './index', uses them with correct props, and demonstrates type safety with different variants and handlers.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created the file, but check that you're importing from './index' and using the components with the correct prop types.
steps.feedbackWrong: The sample usage file is missing or doesn't properly import and use the typed components. Review the import path and prop types.
